People who are related to the event

Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation

I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

issues.item: Triggers: Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
issues.explanation: The loss-themed trigger is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner. It implies bereavement-related activation, but there are no corresponding memory, threat, or appraisal items about death, losing a loved one, or grief. In this profile it stands out as clinically mismatched rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: Avoiding authority figures or uniforms is not well linked to the reported trauma type or the rest of the profile. For intimate-partner physical abuse, this strategy would need supporting material suggesting the perpetrator was an authority figure or that uniforms became trauma cues, but no such trigger, threat, memory, or appraisal items are present. It therefore looks disconnected from the formulation and symptom pattern.

vignette: Tane, a 63-year-old construction foreman from the Pacific coast, began his life on the hard-wired concrete of a New Zealand suburb. He worked at a large building site, his day defined by the rhythm of cranes and the clatter of hammers. The evening after the day's last shift, Tane's wife-his life partner and the only other constant in his world-took a bottle of wine, and the argument that followed turned violent. He was slammed against a steel beam, his right hand slammed against the edge of a pipe until a bruise bled through the skin. The shock of that moment left his body marked with red, a vivid reminder of the abuse that would haunt him for decades. When he thinks of the night, his mind is flooded with images of his own bruised arm and the blackened hands of his former lover; those body parts become the visual triggers that will haunt him. From that night onward, Tane found himself constantly on edge. Ordinary sounds- the screech of a jackhammer, the distant call of a radio- would startle him so sharply that he flinched, his heart racing. He would wake at the middle of the night to sit up, stare at the ceiling, and check whether the house was still safe. In every new room he entered, whether on the construction site or in a friend's apartment, he would instinctively scan for the nearest exit. Each of these threat-related reactions pushed him toward a set of maladaptive strategies. He made a habit of staying near the exits on the job site, always positioned on the far side of the scaffold from the crane operator, and avoided any confrontation that might lead to a disagreement. When a co-worker asked for a raise or a change in schedule, Tane would back away, his eyes darting toward the nearest egress. He also began spending impulsively-buying new work boots, a high-end coffee maker, a new phone- each purchase a frantic attempt to distract himself from the terror that gnawed at his thoughts. The more he bought, the more he felt like a weak, incapable man, unable to control his own life or rely on himself. These maladaptive behaviors, in turn, deepened Tane's negative appraisals. Each time he left the site, the act of scanning exits reminded him of the moment his partner had forced him to the edge of a concrete slab. He began to believe he was inherently weak, that he could not rely on his own judgment. The sense of emotional numbness grew, and he felt as though a dead inside, a void where the warmth of human connection once lived. The compulsion to spend became a further testament to his self-perceived weakness; he justified each purchase as a way to regain control, yet each impulse only reinforced his belief that he could not rely on himself to keep himself safe. Tane's avoidance strategies kept him from confronting the memories that were the roots of his anxiety. The very triggers that prompted his escape-the sight of bruised flesh, the mention of the abusive night-also pushed him further into the safety of his own routines. By staying near exits, he limited his exposure to potentially dangerous situations, but this routine also reinforced his belief that he could never rely on his own strength. The more he avoided conflict, the less he experienced the social reinforcement of a supportive community; this isolation, in turn, made the emotional numbness more profound. When Tane was asked to give a brief speech to a group of apprentices on site, he avoided eye contact, his hands trembling. He tried to stay close to the exit of the building, a position he had always found reassuring. The sound of the apprentice's questions startled him, causing him to startle, to hear his own heart pounding. He felt a surge of panic that reminded him of that night, and the urge to flee again rose to the surface. He also found himself impulsively buying a new set of work gloves the next day, a purchase that left him feeling guilty and more convinced that he was a weak person. The cycle tightened: trigger leads to threat perception, threat leads to avoidance, avoidance reinforces the negative belief that he cannot rely on himself, which in turn fuels more avoidance and compulsive spending, which feeds back into the perception of threat and the vivid triggers. Tane's work life had begun to fray. He was no longer able to take the lead on projects, citing "concerns about safety" to his manager. His relationships with colleagues grew strained, as his avoidance of conflict left him appearing uncooperative. The emotional numbness that had settled in his chest made even casual conversations feel like a test of his supposed weakness. The night after the most recent break in a conversation with a co-worker, Tane finally sought help. He realized that the compulsive spending was draining his savings, that his fear of confronting a simple disagreement had robbed him of the confidence that once made him a respected foreman. What he feared most was the permanent loss of his identity as a capable, reliable man; what he hoped for was a chance to reclaim that sense of self and to stop the relentless cycle of triggers, threats, and avoidance that had become his daily reality.
